title: PageRank: The Random Surfer Model

paper.title: The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web

hook: How does a search engine decide which page is most important? Imagine a random surfer who clicks links forever. The fraction of time spent on each page is its PageRank. Adjust the link structure and damping factor to see how ranks change.

symbols.meaning: Damping factor: probability the surfer follows a link instead of jumping randomly.
Number of pages in the graph.
Adjacency matrix: A[i][j] = 1 if page i links to page j, else 0.
PageRank vector: r[i] is the importance score of page i.
PageRank vector after k iterations of power iteration.

equation.caption: PageRank equation: r is the stationary distribution of a random surfer with damping factor d. D is the diagonal matrix of out-degrees. We use this standard form; the paper's notation may differ slightly.

controls.label: Link matrix A (row i -> column j)

steps: \text{For } k=0,1,\dots: \quad r^{(k+1)} = d \, A^T D^{-1} r^{(k)} + \frac{1-d}{N} \mathbf{1}

explorations.title: Effect of damping factor
explorations.predict: What happens to the PageRank scores when d is set to 0?
explorations.observe: All pages have equal rank (0.25 each).
explorations.why: When d=0, the equation becomes r = (1/N) * 1, so every page gets the same rank regardless of links.

explorations.title: Effect of link structure
explorations.predict: If we change the link matrix so that P3 has many incoming links, how does its rank change?
explorations.observe: P3 gets a higher rank than others because it receives links from P2 and P4? Actually in this cycle, all pages have equal rank.
explorations.why: In a symmetric cycle, each page has one incoming link, so ranks are equal. To see the effect of many incoming links, try a star graph.

self_tests.name: d=1 with default graph: P3 has highest rank
self_tests.expect: out.r[2] > out.r[0] && out.r[2] > out.r[1] && out.r[2] > out.r[3]

limitation: This toy model uses only 4 pages and a simplified link matrix. Real web graphs have billions of pages, and the damping factor is typically set to 0.85. Also, we assume no dangling nodes (pages with no outgoing links) by redistributing uniformly, but the original paper handles them differently.
misconception: Many people think that a page with many outgoing links is important. In PageRank, importance comes from incoming links, not outgoing links.

claims.text: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random surfer with damping factor d.
The PageRank equation is r = d A^T D^{-1} r + (1-d)/N 1.
In our toy setup, we use a 4-page graph and power iteration to compute ranks.

outcomes.outcome: Explain how the damping factor d affects the PageRank scores.
Compute PageRank scores using power iteration on a small graph.
Verify that the PageRank scores sum to 1.
Interpret the link matrix and its effect on ranks.
